name: 裏でやって創 (Ura de Yatte Sou)

claims.text: Standard ramen kitchen: wheat noodles, wheat-based soy-sauce tare, and shared fryer/oil for gyoza and chicken wings mean heavy gluten cross-contact throughout. No GF handling indicated on any source.
Signature bowls include a rich shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, and Japanese soy sauce is standardly brewed with wheat. Assume wheat present in the tare/broth.
Meat-forward menu (Matsusaka-beef hormone ramen) at the back of a yakiniku/offal restaurant; broths and tare are animal/fish based. No plant-based options found.
As a traditional seafood izakaya, grilled shellfish and sashimi are commonly served with or dipped in standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The kitchen centers entirely on shellfish and seafood, so any shared surfaces, grills, and broths should be assumed to involve fish/shellfish.
Much of the menu is whole shellfish grilled shell-on over charcoal, so the core food is naturally simple and unbreaded — a diner who skips soy/sauce can ask for it plain.

name: 粗挽き蕎麦 トキ (Arabiki Soba Toki)

claims.text: Restaurant serves chicken tempura made from Oyama chicken and shrimp tempura as side orders alongside the soba — confirming wheat-battered deep-fried items prepared on premises (shared-fryer / wheat-flour cross-contact risk).
claims.source: https://retty.news/35062/ (via web search of 粗挽き蕎麦 トキ menu)

claims.text: The shop's sauce/broth is described as containing a generous amount of dashi with kombu, sweet and fragrant with strong umami — a traditional dashi-based tsuyu with no indication of wheat-free soy sauce; standard soba tsuyu uses wheat-containing shoyu.

General Tokyo GF guidance flagged for this exact shop context: soy sauce contains wheat and appears in broth, dipping sauces, and seasoning; diners must confirm broth ingredients and ask about gluten-free soy sauce — i.e., no confirmed wheat-free tsuyu here.
No results for this shop on FindMeGlutenFree/HappyCow and no celiac or 'got glutened' reviews located anywhere — no independent corroboration of any GF handling.
Venue is a soba-and-sake izakaya serving ~20 rotating junmai sake with appetizers and course menus including chicken tempura and grated-yam sets — broad non-GF, non-vegan menu with shared prep.
All soba served at the restaurant is made from 100% coarsely-ground buckwheat flour, with no wheat flour blended into the noodle dough itself.

name: 浅草鳩家 ヴィーガンフルーツサンド (Asakusa Hatoya Vegan Fruits Sand)

claims.text: No source reviewed confirms a gluten-free bread option; the standard bread appears to be conventional wheat bread with only the dairy/egg removed, not the gluten.

The shop's stated selling point is that it uses no egg or dairy anywhere in its bread or cream, since it is a dedicated all-vegan fruit-sandwich specialty stall (not a mixed menu alongside animal-based items).
Both the bread and the whipped cream are made from soy milk instead of dairy and egg, so the shop is positioned as safe to eat for vegans and for people with egg or milk allergies.
Compared with a standard dairy-cream fruit sandwich, the soy-cream version is described as roughly a third of the calories and near-zero cholesterol.

Course menus include tempura and dishes seasoned with wheat-containing soy sauce; the restaurant is unable to modify set courses for gluten-free or gluten-allergy requests. Guests seeking to avoid wheat are told to book à la carte and pick dishes themselves.
The restaurant's course menus use soy sauce, which contains wheat.
Due to the ingredients and broth used (including animal-derived dashi/soup), the restaurant is unable to accommodate vegetarian, vegan, or halal orders or modify dishes for these diets.
For gluten-free dining, the restaurant recommends reserving the à la carte menu so guests can select individual dishes themselves, rather than offering a modified or verified allergy-safe course.
The signature soba noodles are handmade from 100% stone-ground buckwheat with no wheat flour binder (juwari soba), milled fresh each morning.

name: 浅草名代らーめん 与ろゐ屋 (Asakusa Nadai Ramen Yoroiya)

claims.text: No gluten-free noodle, soy-sauce, or preparation option is advertised anywhere in the menu information found, including for the vegan ramen; standard wheat noodles and wafu shoyu tare appear to be used throughout.

The vegan ramen is a distinct menu item made in a shop that otherwise cooks meat- and fish-based broths (pork bone, chicken, niboshi, katsuobushi) on the same line; no statement about separate vegan-only equipment or pots was found.

The vegan ramen's broth is described as made entirely from vegetables and kombu (Chinese cabbage, onion, dried shiitake, kombu, carrot) with no animal-derived dashi, and the noodles used for it are egg-free.
The gyoza is made without pork or garlic, using Oyama chicken thigh and harusame (glass noodles), which may suit some dietary preferences though the wrapper is wheat-based.

name: 浅草おでん大多福 (Asakusa Oden Otafuku)

claims.text: No gluten-free protocol, dedicated fryer, or wheat-free broth option is mentioned in any source; the shop is a traditional oden restaurant with no stated allergy accommodations.
The signature broth is seasoned with usukuchi (light) soy sauce, a wheat-containing product, per the shop's own description of its dashi.
The base dashi is made from katsuobushi (bonito flakes) and kombu, meaning the broth itself is not vegan and would flavor any vegetable ingredients cooked in the same pot.
The restaurant's dipping sauce follows classic Edo-mae style — a rich, aromatic tsuyu built on a concentrated soy-sauce base, characteristic of the Kanda Yabusoba lineage.
The menu is built around duck (kamo) — cold kamo-jiru soba and hot kamo nanban are among the most recommended dishes — alongside chicken nanban and sesame-broth soba.
